title: Selectivity Versus Stability of Electrospun Polystyrene Membranes for Hypersaline Brine Separation by Membrane Distillation: A Four-Test Diagnostic Framework
content: Reliable evaluation of membranes for hypersaline desalination requires an integrated assessment of selectivity, transport behaviour and operational stability. This study develops a four-test diagnostic framework combining water-activity calculations, permeate ionic ratios, final-period flux analysis, and hydraulic and thermal characterisation. The framework is applied to electrospun polystyrene (PS), PS membranes containing polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) particles, and commercial PTFE and polyethylene membranes in direct contact membrane distillation of synthetic brines containing 37.8 and 75.7 g L⁻¹ total dissolved solids. Water-activity calculations establish a predicted salinity-related flux reduction of 2.5–5% under the assumed membrane-surface conditions, providing a baseline for interpreting measured flux ratios and temporal behaviour. Final-period analysis resolves start-up effects, yielding commercial PTFE C1/C2 flux ratios of 0.47–0.84. Most PS specimens exhibit low permeate ionic concentrations and chloride-based apparent rejection of 99.987–99.9975%, whereas feed-like ionic ratios in commercial PTFE permeates indicate liquid-feed carryover. Flux–flow exponents of 0.33–0.35 highlight the contribution of external heat transfer. Water-breakthrough pressures of 1.7–7.0 psi and a storage-modulus decrease at 35–55 °C identify priorities for reinforcement and thermal stabilisation. The framework connects separation performance with operating constraints, supports meaningful membrane comparisons, and guides the development of reproducible PS membranes with high selectivity and improved operational robustness.
